newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: World leaders salute Nicaragua's "virtual president". [CORRECTED 23:08 GMT]
newsitem.headline: World leaders salute Nicaragua's "virtual president". [CORRECTED 23:08 GMT]

text.p: Right-winger Arnoldo Aleman's disputed win in Nicaragua's Oct. 20 presidential vote appeared a "done deal" on Sunday as world leaders rallied to congratulate him for his victory.

Aleman has received the congratulations of U.S. President Bill Clinton for his win and the leaders of 21 Spanish-speaking countries meeting in Santiago, Chile, this weekend are set to sign a document on Monday giving the thumbs up to Nicaragua's elections.

On Sunday (corrects from Monday), the presidents of Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Panama released a statement from Chile saying that they categorically supported the recent election, saying it was universal, secret, free and direct.

With the world and powerful sectors of Nicaraguan society acknowledging Aleman as president-elect, the left-wing Sandinista Front's rebellion against the vote's results as illegitimate and fraudulent has become isolated and apparently hopeless.

The official final vote count, released on Friday, gave Aleman an easy 51 to 37.7 percent lead over Sandinista leader Daniel Ortega. But the Sandinistas have said they will appeal the results, demanding that new elections be held in the populous departments (provinces) of Managua and Matagalpa.
Ortega said at a massive protest rally late on Friday that his party "holds the moral and political right to consider these elections illegitimate."
Nicaragua's Supreme Election Council will rule on the appeal and announce official winners by mid-November at the earliest.
But the council's announcement now appears a formality, with President Violeta Chamorro, the Catholic Church and the Nicaraguan business community openly calling Aleman president- elect.
In Clinton's letter, released on Sunday by Aleman's Liberal Alliance, he called Nicaragua's democratic transformation "one of the proudest chapters in the hemisphere's recent history."

"I look forward to cooperating closely with you to continue President (Violeta) Chamorro's successful efforts to promote national reconciliation, strengthen democratic institutions, protect human rights and develop a market economy," Clinton said in the letter to Aleman.

While the United States was officially neutral in the Nicaraguan elections, the memory of the eight-year civil war between U.S.-backed Contra rebels and the left-wing Sandinista government headed by Ortega in the 1980s remained.
Similarly, the final declaration of the VI Ibero-American Summit in Santiago will recognise "the transparency of Nicaragua's electoral process," Nicaragua's Foreign Ministry said.

"We wish to express our pleasure with the recent elections held in Nicaragua, which constitute a fundamental element in the consolidation of democracy in Central America," the signed declaration will say.

The Spanish-speaking presidents will also call on the president-elect to "continue the path of democratization and national reconciliation" started by current Nicaraguan President Violeta Chamorro, the Foreign Ministry said.

Adding insult to injury for the Sandinistas, who governed Nicaragua from 1979 to 1990 with Soviet and Cuban backing, is that one of the leaders scheduled to sign the document is longtime Cuban leader Fidel Castro, Latin America's only remaining Marxist president.
Barring a surprise ruling in favour of the Sandinistas, Aleman will don the presidential sash on Jan. 10, with right-wing businessman Enrique Bolanos as his vice president.
